articles.title_orig: Huge Riots and Anti-Government Protests in France: What to Know
articles.title_zh: Huge Riots and Anti-Government Protests in France: What to Know
articles.content_orig:
Paris police have arrested 855 people after violent clashes during a protest against rising living costs
PARIS -- Paris police said Sunday that 855 people were arrested in the French capital region after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during a protest march that drew about 110,000 people who denounced rising living costs and poor conditions in schools .
Violent clashes, fires and looting on Saturday marred demonstrations across France . Authorities said groups of masked protesters targeted public buildings, including city halls and local government offices.
Authorities said about 550,000 people took part in protests across France, while organizers counted about 800,000.
One person died of a heart attack, Paris police said in a statement, without providing further details. French media reported a protester suffered a medical emergency in the street during the march.
Thirteen police and gendarmerie officers and two firefighters were injured, the statement said.
Around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday morning, dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass marked the aftermath of the events. Looting and damage were reported around the square and in some other tourist and shopping areas in the city center.
Police said groups numbering from several hundred to more than 1,000 people formed unauthorized marches across central Paris on Saturday. “By late afternoon, a new phase began with the arrival of large numbers of people whose sole aim was to steal and loot, taking advantage of the unrest,” police said.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez attributed some of the violence to “radical far-left groups” and said others later joined to loot.
“Peaceful demonstrations have every place in our Republic. Arson, looting and attacks do not,” Lecornu said in a message posted on X.
The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon, the country's three largest cities, requested a meeting with the prime minister in the coming days “given the extent of the damage and the seriousness of the situation.”
In the southern port city of Marseille, some protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall and a police station was damaged. In Lyon, a fire broke out inside a tourist office.
In the central town of Limoges, the City Hall was set on fire, gutting the 19th-century building and collapsing the roof. Haute-Vienne prefect Maurice Barate told LCI television that the blaze, which was under control Sunday, was deliberate.

articles.title_orig: Second Possible Chinese UUV Mothership Appears In Guangzhou
articles.title_zh: Second Possible Chinese UUV Mothership Appears In Guangzhou
articles.content_orig:
Home » Second Possible Chinese UUV Mothership Appears In Guangzhou
New imagery circulating on social media has revealed a second new naval auxiliary vessel for PLAN. Observers speculate the design serves as a Chinese UUV mothership, capable of supporting very large drones through onboard equipment. Naval News provides a brief outline on what the pictures in question add to our existing knowledge of this intriguing development for the Chinese Navy.
The photos in question are stills taken from two very short video reels shared originally on Chinese social media, specifically Weibo. The new pictures quickly spread onto other sites and forums, including “X”, formerly Twitter. The authenticity of these reels remains to be confirmed. Checks with multiple AI detection tools suggest the material is genuine, although superficial “enhancements” cannot be ruled out.
The footage shows several tugboats towing the new auxiliary vessel. The ship carries extensive scaffolding and is still missing all sensor and communication equipment. The location is the Pearl River in Guangzhou, specifically a section near the Panyu district, as the distinct GAC HQ for research and development, known as GAEI headquarters, is visible in the background. One plausible origin of this new vessel is the COMEC shipyard associated with Huangpu Wenchong, on Longxue Island further downstream. However, both the identity of the builder and the destination for further fitting-out work need to await additional imagery for confirmation. At least two other yards belonging to Huangpu further up-river are plausible candidates to finish the fitting-out work. One of these is Huangpu’s primary yard for a wide range of naval vessels, including frigates, surveillance vessels, the Zubr-class LCAC designated as the Type 728 in China, and a recently revealed trimaran submersible .
Naval News previously reported on a new type of presumed Chinese UUV mothership under construction at Hudong, Shanghai. That ship, with a length slightly exceeding 200 metres , features twelve distinct lifting masts at the stern. The assumed purpose of this mechanism is to vertically move a cradle integrated into the ships’s welldeck-like stern. Notional dimensions of this cradle as observed at the yard in Shanghai would enable the device to carry large payloads with a length of up to 50 metres for launch and recovery at sea. Satellite imagery suggests that China is evaluating at least two very large UUV designs between 35 and 45 metres. Such a size renders these vessels the largest known military UUVs in the world.
The new ship now seen in Guangzhou does differ from the unit in Shanghai in several points. The hull appears shorter and narrower, producing an overall smaller vessel. Initial observation suggests a length closer to 150 metres. The jack-up masts at the stern are of a different configuration. Instead of twelve masts, two abreast, at different height like on the Shanghai-built ship the Guangzhou unit only features six extended masts of similar height in a similar two abreast-layout. Both ships share a raised forward deckhouse accommodating the bridge at the front and a large opening leading into a hangar-like area at the rear.
Propulsion mirrors the Shanghai-unit, with side by side smokestacks for diesel engines at the rear of the forward deckhouse. The appearance of the engine exhausts shows minor differences between both vessels, likely owing to differences in total installed power. The Guangzhou-built design includes a relatively conventional hull with an inward cant on the upper hull limited to the deckhouse. Meanwhile the vessel in Shanghai shows a distinctly inwards angled upper hull beginning near the bow and extending over the entire length of the ship. Both ships feature an opening similar to a well deck gate at the stern.
The suspected shipyard for the second Chinese UUV mothership is COMEC, formerly known as GSI. The yard has engaged in significant activity building a range of auxiliary vessels for the Chinese Navy over the last few years. Most notable among these are two sets of amphibious barges the yard assembled since around 2024. Observers associate these designs with a support role for a notional amphibious invasion of Taiwan.
COMEC also continues to build fleet replenishment ships for PLAN, including a second batch of Type 903A AOR. Most recently the yard launched the first hull of a new design of supply vessel. This AOR is similar to but larger than the two Type 901 fleet replenishment ships supporting Chinese carriers. A second hull of this type with a displacement of around 65,000 tons now appears to be under construction at the yard as well. Other recent projects include two new types of submarine support vessels, an experimental carrier-like flattop hull apparently intended for evaluation of UAVs and the third unit of the Type 920 hospital ship, commissioned in 2025.
The purpose of this new auxiliary is likely going to leave room for speculation for a considerable time. The Chinese military is rarely in the habit of sharing significant amounts of information on new construction projects. This is particularly the case for more dedicated or unusual roles. Further assessment needs to await more detailed imagery in order to clarify the intended purpose of these bespoke vessels with the Chinese Navy.

articles.title_orig: Apple Reveals iPhone Duo's Battery Capacity
articles.title_zh: Apple Reveals iPhone Duo's Battery Capacity
articles.content_orig:
Apple on Friday published an EU energy label for the iPhone Duo that reveals the device has a total battery capacity of 4,883 mAh.
The document appears to confirm a previous leak that showed the iPhone Duo has 2,962 mAh and 1,921 mAh battery cells totaling 4,883 mAh. iPhone Duo is an eSIM-only device, so this battery capacity figure should apply worldwide, as there is no version of the device with a physical SIM card tray that would have a slightly smaller battery.
For comparison, iFixit found the eSIM-only iPhone 18 Pro has a 4,288 mAh battery capacity, and the eSIM-only iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 5,567 mAh battery.

articles.title_orig: Several dead or injured in major fire at Canada military base
articles.title_zh: Several dead or injured in major fire at Canada military base
articles.content_orig:
Several people have been killed or injured as a result of a large fire near a Canadian military base in Alberta, the nation's military has said.
The Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) said the full extent of the incident was being assessed and that details of casualties and injuries would not be made public until that was complete.
Canadian TV network Global News reported that at least seven were killed and dozens more injured when a gas line or gas well was hit during a live-fire training exercise, citing unnamed military sources.
Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, where the fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday, is one of the country's busiest military training bases.
On Sunday morning, a defence department spokeswoman told the BBC that "the situation continues to evolve" and "the full extent of the impact remains under assessment".
She also said investigations are in progress but "at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".
Defence Minister David McGuinty earlier said the CAF and local authorities were managing the fire, describing the situation as "very, very active and delicate".
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said his "thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected".
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) said Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton had declared a code orange, a disaster response protocol for responding to a high-casualty incident.
Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor there, told the broadcaster that the number of patients would otherwise "overwhelm" Edmonton's healthcare facilities.
"It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."
After the fire erupted on Saturday, it "spread rapidly due to high winds" and tore through the fences of the base, the Municipal District of Wainwright said.
The region experienced gusts of up to 100km/h (62mph), though local officials indicated fire crews had contained the blaze.
McGuinty told reporters he "cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory".
Local authorities have urged residents to avoid the area and give all emergency vehicles right of way.
The mayor of the nearby town of Wainwright, Bruce Pugh, said it was a "heavy day" for his community.
"We have neighbours who are either serving or former members of the Canadian Armed Forces. We're integrated, our kids play in the same hockey teams, attend the same schools," he told CBC.
While details on the impact of the fire remain unclear, Pugh said he believed this would come to be the area's largest-ever mass casualty event.
Gen Jennie Carignan, chief of Canada's defence staff, said it was a "profoundly difficult moment" for the CAF.
Neighbouring provinces have mobilised in support. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said he had deployed resources to Alberta and was "ready to provide more if required", while British Columbia Premier David Eby said his government had offered "all possible assistance".
Wainwright is the main base used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, according to CBC, with about 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers on-site on a typical day.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo tells faithful in St. Peter's Square he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo tells faithful in St. Peter's Square he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery
articles.content_orig:
The surgeon who operated on Pope Leo XIV earlier this week detailed in an interview with Vatican News how the pope's cancer was discovered, moments before and after his surgical procedure and the importance of prevention.
The pope was discharged from the hospital Saturday — four days after his surgery — to a large crowd of well-wishers cheering for him.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, director of the thoracic surgery unit at the Agostino Gemelli University Hospital Foundation, spoke to the Vatican News in a lengthy interview and said the pope's lung cancer was discovered "entirely by chance."
"The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance — not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora said.
Margaritora said the tumor was found at the base of the right lung, but if it had been "a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen."
Unfortunately, the doctor said, in its early stages, cancers can show no symptoms — such as the lung cancer the pope was diagnosed with. That's why regular preventive checkups for other cancers are so important, he said.
"He had no respiratory symptoms and felt perfectly well," said Margaritora.
The 71-year-old pontiff revealed the news at the end of his Sunday noon blessing last week before thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
Margaritora said the operation to remove a lung nodule was routine and went forward "without any complications." The pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma , a common cancer, during the surgery.
The doctor said that for the four days the pope recovered at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, he was "an ideal patient."
"I am not saying that to flatter him. He truly did not cause the slightest problem for the team caring for him ... ," the doctor told Vatican News.
He said on the second day following the surgery, medical staff found the pope arranging the chairs in the hospital's makeshift chapel. Margaritora recounted that staff offered to move the chairs, "Holy Father, we can do that." And he replied, "It doesn't matter. I can do it, so I will."
The pope had already resumed some work activity on Thursday. By Friday, the pope had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone. Pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small hospital chapel, were released by the Vatican.
He also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. The pope is scheduled to travel Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

articles.title_orig: 4 red flags – and 1 truth – amid the peptide hype
articles.title_zh: 4 red flags – and 1 truth – amid the peptide hype
articles.content_orig:
We traced the patent and development histories of 25 popular compounds, uncovering ties to the pharmaceutical industry far deeper than their reputation suggests.
Peter Attia By: Taylor Yeater, Nicholas Nelson, Lauren Fritsch, Peter Attia
Over the past year, we have returned several times to gray-market peptides—what the evidence actually shows for compounds like BPC-157, CJC-1295, and others—and what we know, or more often do not know, about their safety and efficacy.
In response, we keep hearing some version of the same arguments: “Of course these compounds have not been properly studied. Peptides are difficult or impossible to patent, pharmaceutical companies have little incentive to spend the money required to develop them, and the gray market is left with exceptional therapeutics that conventional pharma has ignored—not because they do not work, but because there is no money to be made proving that they do.”
It’s a persuasive argument. It turns the absence of clinical evidence from a liability into part of the defense. But does it hold up?
We have addressed pieces of this argument before, perhaps too abstractly, because those same (incorrect) claims keep coming back. So rather than simply tell you that peptides can be patented and that many of these compounds have substantial ties to the traditional pharmaceutical industry, we decided to show you—peptide by peptide.
Here, we trace the patent and pharmaceutical-development histories of 25 familiar gray-market peptides, including BPC-157, TB-500, GLP-1 agonists, growth hormone secretagogues, melanocortin peptides, and others. If the story being told holds up, we should have no trouble finding evidence for it across 25 of the most popular gray-market peptides—right?

articles.title_orig: Microsoft pulls plug on Nscale data centre deal
articles.title_zh: Microsoft pulls plug on Nscale data centre deal
articles.content_orig:
Development by UK firm Nscale heralded by ministers as largest of its kind in country loses anchor tenant
The development of a huge AI datacentre hailed by the UK government has received a fresh setback after Microsoft pulled out of the project over concerns about power supplies.
The development by the British company Nscale, heralded by ministers as the country’s largest AI datacentre when it was announced in 2025, was planned to open at Loughton in Essex next year.
Doubts had already emerged about the scheme after the Guardian revealed in March that the location was still an operational scaffolding yard .
Now there are further concerns after Microsoft, one of its largest planned customers and expected to have been the anchor tenant, informed the company that it was pulling the plug on its agreement.
It comes a month after it emerged that power supply problems meant the project would face a lengthy wait before coming online.
Keir Starmer’s government had highlighted the Loughton project when announcing the UK’s AI strategy in 2025 , describing it as the “largest UK sovereign AI datacentre”. Datacentres are the central nervous system of AI technology such as chatbots.
The end of the deal with Microsoft, first reported in the Telegraph, means Nscale has lost its only publicly announced customer for the Essex datacentre. It is understood that Microsoft remains on board for another project the company has in Norway.
Nscale, which is backed by tech companies including Nvidia, has positioned itself as Britain’s “sovereign” datacentre provider but the loss of an anchor tenant for its Loughton project could undermine its ambition to float on Wall Street this year with a potential valuation of $35bn (£26bn).
Targeting the rapid growth of AI to boost the economy, the UK government’s proposals to harness the technology have focused on two Nvidia-backed companies: the London-based Nscale and the US company CoreWeave.
Official figures show investments in AI are among the factors helping Britain’s economy to beat expectations of a weaker growth performance this year as the war in the Middle East rattles global business activity.
Nscale is a “neocloud”, one of a number of companies with deep ties to Nvidia that are building the key infrastructure for the AI boom. It is this relationship with Nvidia that meant it and CoreWeave were chosen as key players in the UK’s sovereign AI push, which happened under Starmer.
There is, however, a growing chorus of voices which suggest that neoclouds may be a vulnerability in the broader AI economy, especially as delays pile up across partners.
after newsletter promotion
Driven by hopes of an economic transformation, many are taking on increasingly risky debt, including companies vital to the AI boom. If Nscale pushes back its initial public offering in New York, these vulnerabilities may come into sharper focus.
The former UK deputy prime minister Nick Clegg and the former Meta chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg are board members at the company. Clegg holds a 0.25% stake that could be worth $88m if the company floats at a $35bn valuation.
It emerged earlier this month that UK Power Networks (UKPN), which owns and maintains the electricity grid across London and the south-east of England, had informed Nscale that it would not be able to supply enough power to the company’s Loughton datacentre until the early to mid-2030s.
Nscale said it was “committed to the project” but the failure to find a quick fix to the power supply issue underlines how much energy has become a hindrance to datacentre development.
The scaffolding yard site has been cleared by Nscale, and the company is investigating whether it can generate power onsite and whether it can speed up the connection process.
An Nscale spokesperson said: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK.
“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”

articles.title_orig: Roth conversions: When the ‘juice isn't really worth the squeeze,’ according to a top-ranked advisor
articles.title_zh: Roth conversions: When the ‘juice isn't really worth the squeeze,’ according to a top-ranked advisor
articles.content_orig:
Roth individual retirement account conversions can potentially reduce lifetime taxes . But the strategy isn't right for everyone, and the choice is now more complex amid updates from President Donald Trump 's "big beautiful bill" and other changes.
Roth conversions transfer pretax or nondeductible IRA funds into a Roth IRA, which kick-starts tax-free growth. The trade-off is that they can trigger more income in the year of the conversion.
The move can be attractive if you have large pretax retirement balances and you expect higher tax rates when it's time to withdraw the funds , experts say.
At year-end 2025, IRA-owning households in the U.S. had $15.9 trillion in assets in traditional IRAs, compared with $2.4 trillion in after-tax Roth IRAs, according to a 2026 report from the Investment Company Institute, an investing trade organization.
Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors:
Weighing Roth conversions, or partial Roth conversions, is "a strategy that continues to be very popular year-over-year," said Charissa Anderson, a certified financial planner who is an executive vice president at Ferguson Wellman Capital Management in Portland, Oregon. Her firm ranked No. 52 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026.
As of March 31, Roth conversions were up 41% this year compared with the same period in 2025, according to the latest Fidelity data , based on an analysis of 19.6 million IRA accounts.
But experts say the strategy isn't right for everyone.
"There are just so many variables" when analyzing a possible Roth conversion, said Tommy Lucas, a CFP at Moisand Fitzgerald Tamayo in Orlando, Florida. His firm is ranked No. 44 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026.
These could include when you claim Social Security , your life expectancy and legacy goals , among other factors, he said.
Depending on your tax bracket, "sometimes the juice isn't really worth the squeeze," said Lucas. "And we're going to have to squeeze every single year" because multiple factors can change the analysis.
If you're eyeing a Roth conversion before year-end, here are some key things to consider.
When deciding on a Roth conversion, projections should include the current year's taxes, along with an analysis of future years, financial advisors say.
"The [tax] bracket you see isn't always the rate you pay," because more income could phase out, or reduce, other tax benefits, according to CFP Tommy Blackburn, senior financial planner and partner at Mason and Associates in Newport News, Virginia. He is also a certified public accountant.
As an example, Blackburn pointed to a client in the 22% tax bracket with a child in college. Income from a conversion could trigger taxes above 30% because the client would lose an education tax credit , which is subtracted from their taxes owed, he said.
By comparison, a client in the 10% tax bracket could convert a limited amount under their standard deduction without owing additional taxes for the current year, he said.
More income could also impact temporary tax deductions enacted via Trump's "big beautiful bill," which have varying income phaseouts.
These could include the bigger federal deduction limit for state and local taxes , known as SALT, worth up to $40,400 for 2026, or the $6,000 senior "bonus" deduction , among others.
Retirees should also consider income-related monthly adjustment amounts, or IRMAAs, which increase Medicare Part B and Part D premiums once income exceeds a certain level. The surcharge is based on modified adjusted gross income from two years prior.
Boosting your AGI with Roth conversions can also reduce the premium tax credit , which makes Affordable Care Act marketplace health insurance less expensive.
Earning even $1 more than a certain income limit can threaten eligibility for the credit — known as the "ACA cliff" — and enrollees could owe full premiums for health coverage.
The cliff affects ACA enrollees when household income exceeds 400% of the federal poverty line, which varies by family size. For 2026, those limits are about $63,000 for a single person or $129,000 for a family of four.
That's why marketplace health insurance enrollees should "proceed with caution" before completing a Roth conversion, said CFP Bill Shafransky, a senior wealth advisor with Moneco Advisors in New Canaan, Connecticut.
"This is one of those financial strategies where you really want to dot your i's and cross your t's before acting," he said.

articles.title_orig: TSA quietly reverses benefit for travelers at some US airports — here’s what to know
articles.title_zh: TSA quietly reverses benefit for travelers at some US airports — here’s what to know
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
A recently expanded program that allowed TSA PreCheck members to go through airport security without a ticket has been abruptly rolled back, according to officials at affected airports.
The initiative, known as “Gateside by TSA PreCheck,” was reintroduced in September at 13 locations before being rolled out to hundreds of additional airports across the country earlier this month.
It was brought back 25 years after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks led to increased airport security protocols. The perk allowed members without plane tickets to clear security and access gate areas at certain U.S. airports , reviving a tradition that largely vanished after the attacks.
However, airport officials say the expansion was reversed within days without public notice, including at Denver International Airport, which was among the newly added locations. News outlet KUSA successfully tested the service last week.
“TSA recently returned Gateside by TSA PreCheck operations to the original 13 participating airports, at least for the time being,” Denver airport said in a statement.
Some aviation hubs were left unaware of the change until passengers raised concerns.
At Norfolk International Airport in Virginia, administrators learned the service had been withdrawn after passengers reported issues accessing the booking system.
“We received a few comments on social media and emails from people who said they recently tried to apply via the TSA’s online portal but found ORF was not among the available airports,” the airport’s Chief Marketing and Communications Officer Chris Jones told CNN . “I logged in to check these claims and likewise did not see ORF in the pulldown menu.”
TSA announced the return of the policy with fanfare last month.
“This new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way, bringing back the moments that once defined air travel,” TSA said on its website .
But without an airport listed on the official website, prospective applicants cannot request a pass. The TSA has not publicly explained the sudden reduction in service.
The Independent has contacted the TSA for comment.
At present, online booking is restricted to the original 13 participating locations:

articles.title_orig: U.S. ambassador to Israel calls for "arrest and prosecution" of Heidi Levine's West Bank settler attackers
articles.title_zh: U.S. ambassador to Israel calls for "arrest and prosecution" of Heidi Levine's West Bank settler attackers
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. ambassador to Israel condemned a settler attack during the olive harvest in the West Bank in which an American journalist was beaten .
In a social media post on Saturday, Ambassador Mike Huckabee called the attack on Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine "vicious & cowardly," citing that she is an American citizen and had identified herself as a journalist. Several Palestinians were also injured in Friday's attack.
"Those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS (years) in prison," Huckabee wrote, adding that he had called for a "full investigation, arrest and prosecution" of the assailants.
"Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards," he said, "dishonorable act of senseless violence."
Video of the incident obtained by CBS News showed a group of around 20 masked men clad in black or gray clothes descending a hill from the area of an Israeli settlement outpost into an olive grove near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah.
Video shared by the Israel-based Foreign Press Association showed Levine was surrounded by masked men, pushed to the ground and beaten, and her camera equipment taken from her.
In a statement on Friday, the Washington Post confirmed the attack, saying Levine "was knocked to the ground, repeatedly kicked and robbed of her cameras and phone despite wearing a protective vest marked 'PRESS' and a helmet."
Israel's police and military said they had opened investigations into the incident.
In the wake of the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned "violence against anyone" but referred to the attack as "alleged" and said its circumstances remain unclear.
Levine, an award-winning photojournalist who has covered conflict zones around the world for more than four decades, remains hospitalized in Tel Aviv as she recovers from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack. She said she was forced to the ground and beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.
Dov  Lieber contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Boomers are buying into the promise of monthly income from options ETFs, but there's a tax catch
articles.title_zh: Boomers are buying into the promise of monthly income from options ETFs, but there's a tax catch
articles.content_orig:
Covered call ETFs have gained a following for their ability to generate monthly cash flow. But a tax surprise could be lurking for many investors.
These actively managed funds have different underlying assets and strategies. But the premise is generally the same. Covered call funds hold equities and sell call options or use related derivatives to generate income. Investors receive attractive income yields in exchange for limited capital upside. The tax piece is more complicated, however.
A fund that realizes option premiums, short-term gains or other income still has taxable amounts to distribute. The tax hit can be easy — and costly — for investors to miss, especially since ETFs are typically understood to be tax-efficient investment vehicles, and especially since most investors aren't looking at the tax implications until they receive a 1099-DIV at tax time, the IRS tax document issued by financial services companies to report dividends and related distributions paid to investors during a tax year.
Even if a fund has good returns and a favorable 30-day SEC yield — which measures the net investment income of bond funds or equity funds and is annualized to reflect the yield an investor would expect to earn over the course of a full year — investors need to look under the hood and understand the tax implications of covered call ETFs. "The after-tax net total return might fall below your expectations," said Matthew Smart, chief investment officer at WWM Investments in Chicago.
Here's what investors need to know about covered call ETFs and taxes:
Distributions from covered call funds come in several forms: dividends, capital gain distributions, or non-dividend distributions. The distribution mix can vary by fund and change year to year. Non-dividend distributions are commonly known as return of capital — payment or distribution from a portion of an investor's original principal rather than an economic profit, capital gain, or dividend earnings. And this is where it can get confusing for investors because ROC distributions aren't treated as current income. Instead, they reduce the investment's cost basis by the distribution amount, so they are tax-deferred until shares are sold.
Covered call ETFs take different approaches to distributions. "Some covered call strategies make distributions characterized only as ordinary dividends. Other strategies make distributions that may include all three types. And since investors' individual tax rates vary significantly, there can be a large difference between what investors receive in fund distributions on a pre-tax basis, and what they keep after paying taxes," ProShares wrote in a blog on covered call strategy and tax efficiency.
Some covered call ETF investors are surprised at tax time by the magnitude of the qualified dividends and ordinary income, said Edwin Retter, senior wealth advisor in the Melbourne, Florida, office of Mission Wealth.
They are also confused by the ROC concept. While it seems favorable from a distribution standpoint in the short term, it's investors' own money coming back to them, which reduces the cost basis. Having a lower cost basis generally increases the investor's capital gains tax liability at the time of sale.
"You're not avoiding the taxes; you're just delaying it until you sell," said Aaron Brachman, wealth manager at the Washington Wealth Group of Steward Partners in Washington, D.C.
Investors who decide to purchase a covered call ETF should ideally do so within a tax-deferred account such as a traditional IRA, Retter said. "I don't know how many investors give so much thought to that. They just find out at tax time that they've put it in a less tax-desirable account."
By investing in a covered call ETF through a traditional IRA, investors don't have to worry about taxes until they pull money out of the account. "You can really save a lot of time and taxes by putting it in the right account structure," Retter said.
Investors who want to better understand how taxes come into play in a covered call ETF can use a measurement known as the tax-cost ratio . The Morningstar Tax Cost Ratio measures how much a fund's annualized return is reduced by the taxes investors pay on distributions. Investors can type in the ticker of the fund they are researching on Morningstar.com, click on the price tab, and scroll down to see the tax-cost ratio.
"It is a flexible tool that can help investors easily compare different time periods, different funds, and different categories. Investors pay taxes when they receive a taxable distribution and these costs are just as relevant as the expense ratio in reducing an investor's take-home return," Morningstar wrote in a paper explaining the methodology for the calculation.
For instance, the JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF ( JEPI ) has a three-year tax cost ratio of 3.11, according to Morningstar. That means after-tax returns are reduced by about 3.11 percentage points annually for investors in the highest tax brackets.
Another example is the JPMorgan Nasdaq Equity Premium Income ETF ( JEPQ ). The fund's three-year tax cost ratio is 4.30. By contrast, the Neos S&P 500(R) High Income ETF ( SPYI ) has a three-year tax cost ratio of 0.48.
The tax picture can be very ETF-specific because it depends on how the fund is structured, said Brent Sullivan, an independent tax analyst at Tax Alpha Insider. SPYI has a higher return of capital than some of its peers, lowering the more immediate tax consequences, but there's still a cost-basis and fund growth issue for investors to consider, he added.
It's not just taxes investors have to consider with these funds. "It's good to look at the portfolio returns, and it's good to look at tax consequences, but NAV has to grow faster than the distribution rate," Sullivan said. "The fund's NAV must keep going up to sustain those distributions. It's not magic. The money has to come from somewhere, and it can't just come from new investors," he said.
Investors should also look at a fund's 30-day SEC yield to get a sense of what the company is generating in terms of income. JEPI has a 30-day SEC yield of 7.45%, compared with JEPQ's 11.56%, and SPYI's 0.45%.
Several financial advisors said they aren't fans of covered call ETFs for tax, complexity and other reasons.
With the 10-year U.S. Treasury continuing to hover around 5%, there are more opportunities for investors to find attractive income in bonds , from ultra-short bond funds to corporate bonds.
"I'd rather have a person in a portfolio that's predominantly fixed income and hedge the interest rate risk with 20% to 40% of the portfolio in high-quality growth stocks," said Andrew Urbanski, founder and chief investment officer at N10 Assets in Greenwich, Connecticut. "If the income isn't enough, draw on the principal from the bond or stock portion of the portfolio in a way that's more risk and cost-efficient," he said.
Covered call ETFs do cap an investor's upside. In a taxable account, an investor might instead buy an S&P 500 ETF — or a total market ETF to get more small and mid-cap exposure — collect the dividends, and make systematic withdrawals through small periodic share sales after a year for tax-efficiency reasons, Retter said.
Index-based ETFs generally have lower expense ratios than their actively managed counterparts. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ( VOO ) has an expense ratio of 0.03%. The Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF ( VTI ) also has an expense ratio of 0.03%.
By contrast, JEPI and JEPQ each have an annual expense ratio of 0.35%. SPYI has an expense ratio of 0.68%.
Meanwhile, many of the covered call ETF funds include the large tech stocks such as Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta that have been driving the market's growth, so it is important for investors to know whether these stocks are already well represented in their portfolio.

On Version History: How a bit of military tech changed the way we learn forever.
On Version History: How a bit of military tech changed the way we learn forever.
It used to be so easy to get away with things in school. The teacher, after all, was always turned around writing at the chalkboard! But then came a bit of technology, previously mostly used for military purposes, called the overhead projector. It would change far more than just the disciplinary record of students everywhere.
In this episode of Version History , we tell the story of the overhead projector. David Pierce is joined by The Verge ’s Jake Kastrenakes and Stanford professor Antero Garcia to discuss how overhead projectors were developed, how they made their way into classrooms, and how they changed so much about the way kids learn. They also try to figure out why overhead projectors have mostly gone away, and whether the things that replaced them — from PowerPoint presentations to computer screens to those new-fangled smart boards — actually improved on the OHP.
This is the final episode of the fifth season of Version History , all about the most iconic school tech. Thanks so much for watching, listening, sending feedback, and everything else! Other than the OHP, we also spent this season looking at Oregon Trail , the original Chromebook , the One Laptop Per Child program, the LeapFrog LeapPad , and those ubiquitous Texas Instruments calculators . articles.title_orig: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
articles.title_zh: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
articles.content_orig:
A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys, while France decried the attack as "appalling". Both called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.
But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened, suggesting it was part of a "co-ordinated campaign to smear Israel".
The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look".
It was also condemned by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law".
In Saturday's incident, the European diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.
Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.
The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.
Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice, as well as ensuring the safety of diplomats, journalists and Palestinians.
"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said.
He also said Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for the violence.
France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot echoed those sentiments, calling on Israeli authorities to "urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations".
Poland's foreign affairs ministry also called for a "firm response" from Israeli authorities and for "an end to the spiral of violence in the West Bank".
The EU condemned the attacks, urged Israel to abide by international and human rights law, and end the expansion of settlements.
A spokesperson said that while they acknowledged some Israeli officials had condemned the attacks, they said they still expect "full accountability as well as effective measures" to stop the continued violence against Palestinians and journalists.
Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.
But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters."
"According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.
But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.
It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".
A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."
It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".
Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

Costco is expanding its diaper selection with a new premium brand, but as of now, shoppers won't find it in the retailer's warehouses.
The warehouse club is now offering Kudos diapers exclusively online, with prices starting at $47.99 per package, giving parents who make their purchases through the company's website another option alongside brands such as Huggies, Pampers and Costco's Kirkland Signature.
According to Costco's website, Kudos diapers are available in sizes 1 through 6, with size 1 priced at $47.99 per package, or approximately 34 cents per diaper. Shipping and handling are included, with delivery estimated at five to seven business days.
Unlike many conventional disposable diapers, Kudos products feature a 100% cotton liner that sits directly against a baby's skin instead of a plastic liner, according to the manufacturer.
COSTCO RECEIVES $184M IN TARIFF REFUNDS, SAYS MOST WILL GO TOWARD LOWER PRICES
Diapers on shelves during the grand opening of a Costco Wholesale store in Kyle, Texas, US, on Thursday, March 30, 2023. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Kudos also advertises its diapers as totally chlorine-free and OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified. The company says its products are made without fragrances, lotions, natural latex, parabens or phthalates.
The company's patented DoubleDry technology features two absorbent layers designed to provide more than 12 hours of leak protection, according to the manufacturer.
The brand was founded by Amrita Saigal, an MIT-trained engineer and former Procter & Gamble employee, who set out to develop disposable diapers made with more cotton and less plastic.
Saigal discussed Kudos' growth and expansion into Costco during an October appearance on The World's First Podcast. According to the episode's published description, the company has sold more than 100 million diapers and is on track to generate over $30 million in revenue in 2026.
The addition expands Costco's online baby-care offerings , though the retailer has not publicly confirmed whether it plans to bring Kudos diapers to its physical warehouses.

articles.title_orig: Always on, always listening: New AI devices are pushing legal limits and could put users in jeopardy
articles.title_zh: Always on, always listening: New AI devices are pushing legal limits and could put users in jeopardy
articles.content_orig:
AI wearables that turn nearby conversations into notes are raising a legal question in Massachusetts and New Hampshire: whether temporary speech processing can count as interception under state wiretap laws.
Amazon introduced its Bee Frontier wearable and Bee Eclipse phone attachment on Oct. 15. Frontier, which costs $74.99, can be worn on the wrist or clipped to clothing and is available now. Eclipse attaches magnetically to a phone, starts at $99.99 and is listed as coming soon. A microphone button controls when Bee processes audio, an indicator light shows when it is active, and audio is processed in real time and deleted. Frontier can also be set to turn off after five or 15 minutes without sound.
Apple announced Siri Recap and Live Rewind for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Siri Recap can summarize conversations, while Live Rewind can display text from the previous 15 seconds. Users can enable each feature and set when and where Siri Recap takes notes. The features were slated to enter beta later in 2026.
Audio is deleted after processing. For Siri Recap, encrypted audio moves from the Watch to a paired iPhone for processing, then condensed text is sent to Private Cloud Compute to produce a summary. Live Rewind plays a chime and displays a microphone indicator when activated.
Massachusetts law defines interception as secretly hearing or recording communication content without prior authority from all parties, subject to statutory provisions. New Hampshire law includes the aural or other acquisition of communication content in its definition and restricts willful interception without all parties’ consent, with separate rules for participant interceptions.
Those definitions address hearing or acquiring content as well as recording it, leaving an open question about whether temporary AI processing could qualify even when raw audio is deleted. The statutes do not specifically resolve how that distinction applies to these devices.
A wearer’s consent also may not answer whether nearby people agreed to have their words processed. Karen Panetta, dean of graduate education at Tufts’ School of Engineering and an IEEE fellow, said a wearer’s consent “doesn’t mean everybody else around you has given that consent.” Apple’s features were still slated for beta later in 2026; Amazon’s Bee devices are newly available or listed as coming soon.
Riza Dagoc reports on regulation, investing and the digital-asset business for TokenPost. Send corrections or tips to info@tokenpost.com.

articles.title_orig: On Camera, Priest Crushed Under Massive Crucifix In Front Of Worshippers
articles.title_zh: On Camera, Priest Crushed Under Massive Crucifix In Front Of Worshippers
articles.content_orig:
A Catholic priest died after a large crucifix fell on top of him while he was leading a mass in Ecuador that was being livestreamed at the time.
Footage shared widely on social media shows Father Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari addressing his congregation in Guayaquil on Saturday before the crucifix came tumbling down on top of him and striking him in the head.
The Archdiocese of Guayaquil on Sunday confirmed that Father Sánchez Molinari had died in a post on social media which said: "We announce that our beloved Fr. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari, CSsR., who served as parish priest of Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church in the Central Vicariate, has departed for the Father’s House to rejoice in His presence and glory."
The statement continued: "Eternal rest grant unto him, O Lord. And let perpetual light shine upon him. May he rest in peace. Amen."
The cause of the crucifix's collapse remains currently unknown, with no official explanation issued about if structural damage or faulty fittings contributed to the accident.
Newsweek has contacted the Archdiocese of Guayaquil, via email outside of normal working hours, for comment.
Details on who Father Sánchez Molinari was are sparse. He was the parish priest of Nuestra Señora del Perpetuo Socorro, Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church, and part of the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, founded in 1732 by the Italian St. Alphonsus Liguori. The congregation generally focus serving on poor, isolated communities.
Father Sánchez Molinari was assigned to downtown Guayaquil and had worked in Vinces, Los Ríos Province before, according to local outlet Guayaquil News.
The priest livestreamed Masses from his own social media profiles and YouTube channel.
The Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer was started by Italian St. Alphonsus Liguori, who preached with his colleagues who left his legal career to preach in rural and isolated communities around Naples.
His congregation spread and by the 19th century, there were Redemptorists in Italy, Poland, Germany, Belgium and Holland, according to the Redemptorists’ Baltimore Province’ official page.
Redemptorists started working in the U.S., as their first mission outside of Europe, first  working with Native Americans and then with Irish, German and Slavic immigrants. They often taught immigrants the English language.
Serving immigrant communities has remained a priority for the congregation, which now has around 4,500 members who serve in 82 countries on all five continents.
Their work is inspired by Psalm 130:7 - “In Him there is plentiful redemption.” The congregation is named after a Catholic title for the Virgin Mary, Our Lady of Perpetual Help.

articles.content_orig:
Nothing Bundt Cakes CEO Dolf Berle shares how lessons from a dairy farm shaped his leadership style and why he believes vulnerability helps leaders connect with their teams.
Nothing Bundt Cakes CEO Dolf Berle said that some of the biggest lessons shaping his leadership came long before he reached the C-suite – including from his first job on a dairy farm.
Berle told FOX Business that the "discipline around success routines" he learned through dairy farming still influences how he takes care of himself and runs a business.
"For me, the habit that has made the biggest difference is the discipline around success routines – both in terms of self-care, but also running a business – that came out of my youth in dairy farming," he said.
Before taking the helm of Nothing Bundt Cakes, Berle held leadership roles at Topgolf, Dave & Buster's, Lucky Strike Lanes, House of Blues and ClubCorp.
CEO SUNDAY: TROPICAL SMOOTHIE CAFE CEO SAYS 'LISTENING AND LEARNING' ARE KEYS TO SUCCESS
Nothing Bundt Cakes CEO Dolf Berle told FOX Business that some of the biggest lessons shaping his leadership came long before he reached the C-suite. (Nothing Bundt Cakes )
Berle has earned degrees from Harvard University and the University of Zimbabwe and has won world and national championship medals in pole vault, heptathlon and decathlon. He also competed on "American Ninja Warrior."
Another lesson that has shaped his leadership is the importance of vulnerability.
"The best piece of career advice that I've received is that it's OK to be vulnerable because people connect through vulnerability," he said.
Berle said that openness can help leaders better understand and support their teams.
That approach also shapes one responsibility Berle said he prefers not to delegate, which is delivering difficult news.

"When there's something very difficult or very hard that needs to be conveyed to a partner or to someone you're working with, I like to do that myself because I really want to explain why we're doing what we're doing," he said.
"I want to try to be compassionate around the feelings that this may cause for someone, but also be clear about the fact that what we are doing is for the good of the overall business and the team going forward."
Berle also pushed back on the idea that being a CEO is "glamorous."
"I think some people think that being a CEO is glamorous, and actually that is not the case," he said. "It's a servant role. It's a role that deals with many of the most difficult things."
He added, "It's very meaningful and fulfilling, but I don't think it's glamorous."

articles.title_orig: India’s Middle Power Problem: Hedging Between Russia’s Decline and China’s Rise
articles.title_zh: India’s Middle Power Problem: Hedging Between Russia’s Decline and China’s Rise
articles.content_orig:
In an effort to be in compliance with GDPR we are providing you with the latest documentation about how we collect, use, share and secure your information, we want to make you aware of our updated privacy policy here
In 2026 India concluded a free trade agreement with the European Union, struck an interim tariff deal with the United States, absorbed a Gulf war that upended its oil supply, sent its air force to train with Japanese fighters, and hosted both Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping at a BRICS summit in New Delhi. Eleven days before welcoming Putin, Narendra Modi had told him in Bishkek that the world must move from endless war to an end to the war.
Taken one at a time these are episodes. Taken together they describe a state working every relationship at once. My two recent articles argued that this is hedging rather than realignment. India is thinning its dependence on Russia at the margin while keeping the installed Russian base, buying Russian oil when supply and price justify it, and building partners elsewhere.
This article asks what that pattern means for India as a middle power. It uses the framework Kenneth Maxwell and I developed in The Australian, Brazilian and Chinese Dynamic . My argument is that the Russia hedge is a subordinate move in a larger game. The principal problem is China. Russia matters to India less as a partner than as a counterweight, and as a warning about what China’s informal empire does to a partner it has weakened.
Three findings carry over. First, India’s Russia relationship must be read as stock and flow. The share of new arms deliveries from Russia has fallen from 70 to 40 per cent over a decade, while the installed base remains overwhelmingly Russian in origin. Second, India layers rather than exits. It refused the Su-57 and is upgrading the Su-30MKI with Indian sensors and weapons, but it also ordered more S-400s. Third, Russian oil is a portfolio position, driven by Gulf disruption, Russian supply and American pressure rather than by sentiment about Ukraine.
The Ukraine book supplies the frame around these findings. Putin’s war has shrunk Russia’s reach and made it a junior partner of China. India is the largest Global South customer whose choices decide how far that subordination goes. Its interest is not simply to reduce Russian exposure but to keep Russia from becoming wholly dependent on Beijing while it reduces its own.
Our book offers four ideas that matter here.
Informal empire. Following Gallagher and Robinson’s 1953 concept, we argued that China builds influence through trade, investment, ports, finance and a Global South narrative rather than formal control. Latin America was our main case, but the method is general. It creates dependence through commerce and then converts dependence into political leverage.
Two models. Australia leans toward security when forced to choose. It accepts economic costs, banned Huawei from its 5G network, and built a deterrence-focused defense posture around the alliance with the United States. Brazil practices strategic pragmatism. It embraces Chinese trade, uses BRICS to expand its autonomy, and signed a cooperation plan linking its programs to the Belt and Road rather than joining the initiative formally. We explained the divergence through geography, alliance commitments, history and economic structure.
Hedging as the norm. Both countries hedge, in different versions, and we argued this is becoming normal for middle powers rather than exceptional. We also noted that Beijing courts middle powers with a multi-alignment strategy of its own, encouraging cooperative relations with several powers rather than exclusive alignment. Hedging does not threaten China’s informal empire unless it is backed by capability.
Capability, resolve and signalling. Air Marshal Chipman’s framing of deterrence as capability multiplied by resolve multiplied by signalling, where a zero in any term makes the product zero, applies to any middle power facing a larger neighbor. Resolve, he argued, is a whole-of-society problem that includes economic relationships with the adversary.
By the book’s material definition, India does not qualify. It describes middle powers as economies ranking roughly twentieth to thirtieth, while India’s economy is far larger, and India is nuclear-armed with 1.4 billion people. Yet the book’s concluding chapter lists “the Indians” among the significant middle powers, and the functional definition makes sense. A middle power is a state that cannot decide the order alone and must shape it through partnerships, institutions and selective capabilities. India fits that description relative to the United States and China.
India is a third case that combines features of both of our models. Like Australia, it faces a direct security problem with China. It has a contested land border, the 2020 Galwan clash, and a Chinese military build-up on the Line of Actual Control. Like Brazil, it insists on strategic autonomy, chairs BRICS, and refuses to become a treaty ally. Unlike both, it has neither an alliance guarantee nor Brazil’s geographic distance. Its Russian ties give it a hedge that neither Australia nor Brazil possesses.
The clearest sign is trade. The latest reporting puts India’s trade deficit with China above $112 billion, the widest on record, with imports over $130 billion against exports under $20 billion. Another account says India buys about seven dollars of Chinese goods for every dollar it sells, in a relationship where trade has nearly doubled in five years. Much of this is organic, driven by Chinese price and technology competitiveness, which is exactly how informal empire works. Dependence grows through commerce that appears voluntary.
Leverage follows dependence. Over 90 per cent of India’s rare earth magnets and metals came from China, and Chinese rare earth magnet exports to India fell 58 per cent after January 2025. Earlier this year China also restricted imports of Indian rice and chilli. India’s response includes a Rs 7,280 crore magnet manufacturing scheme approved in November 2025 and rare earth corridors announced in the 2026-27 Budget. These are the right measures, but their effects will take years.
Australia’s experience is instructive. Babbage’s argument in our book is that Chinese coercion of Australia was a “sovereignty war” rather than a trade dispute, and that resilience means diversifying markets and supply chains. A study by Laurenceson that we quote finds that Australia’s interests were protected not by geopolitical friends but by interdependence that constrained Beijing and by access to a rules-based trading system. Diversification worked because alternatives existed.
Russia is the negative example. As the Ukraine book shows, China has made Russia a price-taker, moved it into the yuan, and captured its Far East and Central Asian markets. India has a direct interest in avoiding a similar path.
India has spent 2026 building alternatives, and the record shows a familiar hedging style.
On February 2 President Trump announced a deal cutting US tariffs on Indian goods to 18 per cent and said Modi had agreed to stop buying Russian oil. The joint statement did not mention Russian oil, and the Indian government has neither confirmed nor denied the pledge, saying its purchases are guided by national interest. An executive order provides that a 25 per cent tariff would return if India resumes such purchases. Indian refiners meanwhile avoided Russian cargoes for March and April, and Russian crude’s share of Indian imports had already fallen from a 40 per cent peak to under 25 per cent by December.
Then the Iran war began on February 28. India’s Russian oil share went from 18.7 per cent in February to nearly 50 per cent in July, as its Middle East imports fell by 63 per cent. I have not found reporting that the US has reimposed the tariff, although Senate pressure for tariffs on buyers of Russian energy is growing. The sequence looks like textbook hedging

articles.title_orig: Why stealing pumpkins for newlyweds is a blessing in ancient Chinese tradition
articles.title_zh: Why stealing pumpkins for newlyweds is a blessing in ancient Chinese tradition
articles.content_orig:
Some northern communities traditionally place a pumpkin under the wedding quilt as a blessing for future generations
In ancient China, welcoming autumn could involve stealing pumpkins, sitting on giant hanging scales and eating extra meat – rituals reflecting how people connected seasonal change with fertility, health and good fortune.
Historical records show that during the Qing dynasty (1644–1912), groups of young people would gather on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival to sneak into fields and take pumpkins.
Far from being considered wrongdoing, the practice was often tolerated – and even welcomed – by farmers. By the Republican era (1912–1949), it had become particularly prevalent in rural communities.

articles.title_orig: China to limit exports of 40 key technologies, including AI and solar
articles.title_zh: China to limit exports of 40 key technologies, including AI and solar
articles.content_orig:
China's Ministry of Commerce has released a draft plan for export limits on 40 key technologies in artificial intelligence (AI), photovoltaics and biomedicine.
The export of 14 of these technologies is to be banned, while the other 26 will require approval. The new bans and approval requirements have not yet been finalized. Comments can be submitted until November 15.
However, since the announcement was published on Friday, companies have been required to register affected technology transfers. Such transfers include selling intellectual property rights and granting licences abroad.
The focus is on 23 AI technologies. These include methods for large AI models and AI agents, which perform tasks largely autonomously. Further plans concern manufacturing processes for solar cells and techniques for cell and gene therapies.
Access to AI services via apps and websites is to remain exempt from the new export limits, according to the ministry. This also applies to AI technologies that are already publicly available.
In solar technology, individual production facilities are covered, but finished solar modules will not fall under the planned controls.
The Ministry of Commerce cited security risks. AI could be used for attacks on important infrastructure. Solar technology is also used in space and defence. The measures are not aimed at specific countries or companies.
China had already restricted certain processes for making battery materials and extracting lithium in 2025. Approval requirements were also introduced for certain rare earths and products made from them.
The new move falls into the technology rivalry with the United States, which in turn controls exports of advanced AI chips to China.

articles.title_orig: 4 Takeaways From a Voting-Focused ‘No Kings’ Day
articles.title_zh: 4 Takeaways From a Voting-Focused ‘No Kings’ Day
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of demonstrators rallied and marched near the Colorado Capitol on Saturday in the largest of dozens of planned No Kings events across the state, part of a nationwide day of action that organizers hope will encourage participants to vote and help protect the November election.
It was the latest in a series of No Kings events since President Donald Trump’s inauguration in January 2025. Protesters say the Trump administration has pursued authoritarian policies, such as disregard for the rule of law, abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and attempts to meddle in elections.
Nita Gonzales, daughter of Denver Chicano activist Corky Gonzales and a longtime activist herself, addressed a crowd of hundreds of demonstrators gathered on the Capitol grounds and across Civic Center Park.
“Does this look like hopelessness? This looks like courage,” Gonzales said from the Capitol steps. “This looks like democracy. This looks like people reclaiming their voice and their power.”
Christy Aguilar, an organizer of the Denver rally, told Newsline she wanted the event to engage and represent Colorado’s Latino community in a way that previous events hadn’t.
“I’ve noticed the lack of Latino power in No Kings planning, I’ve noticed (the) Latino population not coming out to No Kings,” Aguilar said. “So this was my way of trying to get my community to come out and get them more involved in the polls, get them more informed of what’s going on. Because everything that’s on the ballot is affecting us personally.”
Nationwide, Saturday’s No Kings protests were focused on mobilizing voters to make a plan for heading to the polls, and to vote early if possible. National No Kings organizers were joined at a press conference in Washington earlier this week by Bishop William Barber, founder of the social justice group Repairers of the Breach and co-chair of the Poor People’s Campaign, who has organized 652 early-voting marches in 428 locations across the country this year.
Under Colorado’s universal vote-by-mail system, ballots were mailed to all active registered voters in the state beginning Oct. 2. Voters may submit completed ballots by mail or at a drop box or voting center. They may also vote in-person at a voting center. Eligible voters can visit GoVoteColorado.gov for more information and to check their registration status.
In an interview, Gonzales said the consequences of Trump’s actions over the last decade have been been “horrific” for the Latino community and beyond.
“I’m a grandmother,” she said. “I don’t want my grandchild being raised in this kind of environment, where those that have more get more, and those that have less are at the bottom of of the rung and not able to have a life that they deserve to have. So then I get angry.”
Mark Lyons of Centennial told Newsline he hadn’t been involved in much political activism or organizing before last year. Saturday’s protest was his fourth No Kings event.
“I thought it’s time to get involved, it’s time to make a difference,” Lyons said. “It’s a community, and a lot of like-minded people, coming together for a common goal.”
I’m a grandmother ... I don’t want my grandchild being raised in this kind of environment, where those that have more get more, and those that have less are at the bottom of of the rung and not able to have a life that they deserve to have. So then I get angry.
– Nita Gonzales, at the No Kings protest
With the midterms approaching, Lyons is hopeful that Democrats will take back Congress and “put all kinds of checks and balances” on the Trump administration.
“They’ve been stealing the country blind for the last two years,” he said. “There has to be accountability, and it can’t be business as usual.”
No Kings event in Grand Junction emphasizes early voting, nonpartisan participation
Protests in Colorado were planned in numerous locations throughout the Denver area, and in cities such as Fort Collins, Boulder, Colorado Springs, Pueblo, Grand Junction and Durango.
“The No Kings movement stands ready to mobilize in response to attacks on our elections,” the No Kings website says. “By signing the No Kings pledge, you commit to be part of the solution, ready to join mass nonviolent action in rapid response to election disruption and subversion if needed.”
Aly Belknap, executive director of Colorado Common Cause, urged rally-goers to help “defend the vote” against the lies about widespread voter fraud promoted by Trump and many other Republicans. Her organization is leading a coalition of groups that are training nonpartisan, volunteer poll monitors to observe polling sites and drop boxes to protect against subversion next month.
“We know that we have debunked this lie over and over and over, and yet these are the lies that constitute what our neighbors and our family members and even our friends have been drawn in to believe,” Belknap said. “Why? … (Because) the people in power, they would like to decide who wins.”
Gonzales told the crowd to vote — “and then after you vote,” she added, “you get yourself out to defend your neighbors and communities, and stand up against ICE.”
“Voting is step one, but it is also about continuing to be active in neighborhoods and communities, to defend your neighbors, stand up, whatever that call comes, and not become complacent,” Gonzales told Newsline. “That’s what went wrong — we got complacent. We have to be vigilant, and we have to protect democracy and freedom, and that means standing up.”

articles.title_orig: What brought a Chinese desert fighter and an American teacher together?
articles.title_zh: What brought a Chinese desert fighter and an American teacher together?
articles.content_orig:
It was Oct 15, and I was at the headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Rome, witnessing FAO honor 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development. Ninety-nine names had been published on its website well in advance, but the organizers had kept the final recipient a secret.
It was a clever but also risky decision, I have to say. Keeping the name secret would help attract global attention, but whoever was chosen would have to live up to the expectations created by such an unusual announcement.
My doubts disappeared the moment the name and photograph of Yin Yuzhen appeared on the giant screen. Huge applause erupted. Journalists and delegates alike rushed forward, hoping to catch a closer glimpse of the Chinese woman who had devoted decades to fighting desertification. The applause quickly turned into a rhythm, with people chanting her name in different accents.
Accompanied by FAO director-general Qu Dongyu, Yin made her way onto the stage.
There she was, standing before an international audience, looking much as she might have looked back home in the countryside of northern China, wearing a dark green top and gray-black trousers. She struggled to work two English words, "brother" and "sister", into her Mandarin acceptance speech, but with such a heavy accent that few caught them.
But that didn't matter. Everyone in the hall knew her story with 8 million trees planted at the Mu Us Sandy Land, an achievement whose weight everyone understood beyond words.
Ronald Sakolsky, a retired American teacher who helped her in the 1990s and kept a 27-year-long friendship with her, joined her. Qu joked that Sakolsky was not eligible for an award honoring women, but had prepared a special souvenir for him.
Sakolsky laughed along with everyone else, but soon found himself in tears as he looked back on how they first met and what they had achieved together. The two spoke onstage, revisiting their past, reflecting on the present and imagining the future, thus turning the ceremony into a deeply moving reunion.
Yet for me, it also raised a question: Yin and Sakolsky's first encounter lasted only a few days, during which Sakolsky, having raised $5,000 for tree planting, visited her to see how she did it. Sakolsky eventually returned to his own life, while Yin went back to planting trees. They did not see each other again for 27 years, until they reunited in China earlier this year.
Yet when they met again, the warmth and understanding between them seemed entirely undiminished.
How could two people who had spent so little time together, and then stayed apart for nearly three decades, still share such a powerful connection?
After interviewing both of them, I think I found the answer: They are both idealists. OK, if the word appears too grand, let's call them people determined to do things well.
A rural woman confronting a desert, Yin has known since the first day she planted trees that every additional tree meant a little more greenery and a little less sand. She has never been taught any grand environmental theory; yet she never lost the belief that if she kept working, the landscape around her could eventually change.
Sakolsky, an American teacher, heard about someone trying to make the planet a better place. He believed such an effort deserved support, even if the person undertaking it lived thousands of kilometers from his home.
For Yin, planting trees was simply the right thing to do. For Sakolsky, helping someone plant them was equally obvious.
In a sense, both were stubborn. Once they had decided what was worth doing, they were determined to do it.
That's what linked them together, across national boundaries, languages and cultures. Such a friendship doesn't need frequent meetings, shared professional interests or expectations of personal reward. It is sustained by a shared belief that ordinary people can improve the world through their own actions.
More importantly, idealism, or the strong belief that one can do things well, is contagious. In our exclusive interview, when recalling 1999, Sakolsky said that he didn't think Yin could succeed until he saw what she was doing with his own eyes. And he is not the only one inspired by Yin, who said the award not only belongs to her alone, but also to the many "brothers and sisters" who helped.
Those "brothers and sisters" include people from the local government, nearby communities, and volunteers from over 20 countries and regions. Many didn't believe someone could plant trees in the sandy land first, but later joined Yin in her resolve.
They, too, were inspired by Yin, and have become idealists ready to inspire others.
Perhaps after spending so much of her life planting trees, Yin simply cannot stop. On Oct 16, the day after the ceremony, she joined Sakolsky and Qu in planting another tree at FAO headquarters.
It was World Food Day, and delegates attending the celebrations gathered around, eager to see this legendary Chinese desert fighter at work. Hopefully, when they return home, more people will continue the path of inspiration.
Of course, not everyone has the opportunity to meet Yin in person, but perhaps that is not necessary. Everyone who continues working toward a worthwhile ideal, however modest the effort may seem, carries something of the same spirit.
And every tree planted, wherever it grows, is another reminder that the world can be made a little better by people who believe it is worth trying.
